title: Shavuot: a night of learning
hook: staying up to learn, even an hour past your bedtime
tomorrow: why does every chapter of Avot start with a borrowed line?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Israel's days: many ways to mark them, or none, and Hillel's line about not judging. Your own way. Now the seven weeks of counting run out, and a festival begins at night.

The alarm goes off once. Nobody moves. It goes off again. Still nothing. Usually that means a missed first period. In this story, it's the morning God is about to speak at Sinai. A midrash tells it plainly: on the morning the Torah was given, the people were still asleep, and they had to be woken up. So why would anyone stay up all night on purpose? To make sure that this time, nobody sleeps through it.
screen: `THE ALARM, TWICE.` → `THE MORNING AT SINAI.` → `THEY OVERSLEPT.`

segments.voice: Exodus makes that morning loud: "And it came to pass on the third day, when it was morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of a horn exceeding loud." Thunder, lightning, a horn. And still, says the midrash, the people had slept in. It's a strangely human detail to keep about the biggest morning in the story. Later Jews answered it with a custom: tikkun leil Shavuot, the repair of Shavuot night. Some stay awake on the first night of the festival, learning until dawn, in a synagogue, a living room, a kitchen with too much coffee. Kabbalists in Safed shaped a set reading for the night, passages from the Torah, the Prophets and the Mishnah. Now it might be a string of short classes, a study partner, or one good page. The repair is the point. Last time they slept; this time we're up, waiting. You don't need the whole night. Even an hour past your bedtime, reading something that matters, on purpose, while the house is dark, is the same gesture in small: I'm here, I'm awake, I don't want to miss it.
screen: `THUNDER, LIGHTNING, A HORN.` · `AND THEY SLEPT IN.` · `TIKKUN: THE REPAIR OF THE NIGHT.` · `EVEN ONE HOUR COUNTS.` · then, large: `AWAKE FOR THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Copy one line by hand from any book that matters to you, slowly, word by word, the way you'd copy a recipe you don't want to lose. Read it back once, quietly. That's the night of learning, in miniature.
screen: `ONE LINE, BY HAND.` · `WORD BY WORD.` · `READ IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Tikkun leil Shavuot: the repair of Shavuot night, staying up to learn so that, this time, no one sleeps through the gift.
Hold this one close: awake for the gift, even for one extra hour. Good night, and good morning.

howItsDone: On the first night of Shavuot, some Jews stay awake learning Torah until dawn, alone, with a partner, or at a synagogue program of short classes; others learn for an hour or two past their usual bedtime.
